q: The number of donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal atom in a complex is called
why: Coordination number counts the sigma bonds from donor atoms to the central metal.

q: Which of the following is an ambidentate ligand?
why: SCN- can coordinate through either S or N, making it ambidentate.

q: The coordination number of Ni in [Ni(CO)4] is
why: Four CO ligands each donate through one C atom, giving CN = 4 (tetrahedral).

q: In IUPAC naming of coordination compounds, if the complex ion is an anion, the metal name ends in
why: Anionic complexes have the metal name suffixed with '-ate', e.g. ferrate, cobaltate.
Ligands are named alphabetically (ammine before chlorido) followed by metal and oxidation state III in brackets.

q: [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] shows cis and trans forms; this is an example of
why: Cis and trans arrangements of the same ligands around a square planar metal is geometrical (stereo) isomerism.

q: In Valence Bond Theory, dsp2 hybridisation of the central metal gives a complex with geometry
why: dsp2 hybridisation uses one d, one s and two p orbitals, giving square planar geometry, e.g. [Ni(CN)4]2-.

q: According to Crystal Field Theory, in an octahedral complex the d-orbitals split into
why: In octahedral field, three t2g orbitals are lower in energy and two eg orbitals are higher, separated by delta-o.

q: Which ligand causes a strong field and favours a low spin octahedral complex?
why: CN- is a strong field ligand causing large delta-o, forcing electrons to pair in t2g (low spin).

q: Cisplatin, used as an anti-cancer drug, has the formula
why: Cisplatin is the cis isomer of diamminedichloridoplatinum(II), used in chemotherapy.
